steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper on multitask learning for node label prediction on graphs, where tasks are clustered into groups using higher-order task affinities in a boosting-style procedure. Motivate the problem and negative transfer, review how task relationships are modeled today, describe our approach and theory, and close with contributions and the paper's organization.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Multiple node labeling tasks on graphs; multitask learning; our boosting idea
- Negative transfer and structural differences on graphs
- Limits of existing task-relatedness / task-affinity methods
- Main contribution: clustering tasks with higher-order affinities
- Approach: affinity scores, spectral clustering, sampling-based estimation
- Theory; summary of contributions; organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem setting
  - predict multiple node label tasks on graphs at once?
  - e.g. supervised, overlapping community detection (cite): seed labels -> does another node belong to community?
  - multi-label learning: labels of multiple communities; predict labels for remaining nodes
  - cast as multitask learning (cite); applications: knowledge graphs (cite), protein-protein interactions (cite)
  - traditional: single model on all tasks (cite)
  - we: task relationships with shared GNN; notable negative transfers
  - fix: boosting procedure, cluster tasks into groups, one GNN per group
- Negative transfer
  - shared encoder can be worse than single-task learning (STL) for a task (cite); seen for many data modalities (cite)
  - causes: heterogeneity in input features, dataset sizes; much less known for graphs
  - two works (cite, cite): structural differences in transfer learning on graphs due to graph diffusion
  - can also cause negative interference in MTL -> need to model structural differences; also for task grouping (cite)
- Existing methods
  - classical MTL: task relatedness via heuristics and theory (cite); doesn't apply to nonlinear NNs
  - naive: search all task combinations -> costly for many tasks
  - prior work (cite): pairwise affinity by training a model per pair; higher-order = average of first-order
  - other methods (cite): first-order affinity via gradient similarity
  - efficient, but ignore higher-order relationships (more than two tasks)
  - higher-order affinities not predictable from first-order (Figure 5, Section 5.1); transfer not monotone or submodular, more task data doesn't always help (Figure 4, Section 3.2)
  - all pairwise: T^{2} models for T tasks, costly even for tens of tasks
- Main contribution
  - efficient algorithm clustering tasks into groups, accounting for higher-order transfer
  - compare: GNN on all tasks vs several multitask GNNs, one per group
  - Section 5: best results among many baselines on real-world datasets
  - boosting procedure (cite), works on top of any graph learning algorithm
- Approach (Figure 1)
  - affinity \theta_{i,j} for each pair i, j; higher = j transfers better to i, with other tasks present
  - like feature importance in random forests with hundreds of other features
  - predicts positive/negative transfer of a set of tasks to a target
  - spectral clustering (cite) on [\theta_{i,j}]_{T\times T}; optimizes sum of within-group affinities
  - estimation: naive O(T^{2}); ours O(T) via sampling
  - n=O(T) random subsets of \{1,2,\dots,T\}, fixed size \alpha (\alpha=5 suffices)
  - fit MTL model per subset; f_{i}(S) = holdout prediction loss of task i given S\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,T\}; measures transfer from S to i
  - \theta_{i,j} = average over subsets containing i,j
- Theory
  - stochastic block model style setting, well-separated tasks
  - planted model: [\theta_{i,j}]_{T\times T} block-diagonal, one block per cluster -> spectral clustering recovers structure
- Contributions: (1) affinity score + sampling, O(T) MTL models; (2) spectral clustering + recovery guarantees; (3) experiments on community detection and molecular graph datasets, better test accuracy than community detection and MTL baselines
- Organization: Sec 2 related work; Sec 3 negative transfer evidence; Sec 4 boosting; Sec 5 experiments; Sec 6 theory; Appendix A proofs; Appendix B more experiments

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Given multiple node label prediction tasks on graphs, can we design a model that predicts all of them at the same time? One example is supervised, overlapping community detection: given a set of labels as a seed set, can we learn to predict if another node of the graph belongs to a community? This is an example of multi-label learning, where the input has labels of multiple communities and the goal is to predict the community labels for the remaining nodes of each community. In this paper we cast this multi-label classification problem into the more general formulation of multitask learning, which also has a lot of other applications in knowledge graphs and protein-protein interactions. Traditionally multitask learning works by fitting one model on all the tasks. Instead, we investigate the task relationships on graphs with a shared graph neural network, and we observe notable negative transfers between different tasks. To address this, we design a boosting procedure that clusters tasks into groups and then fits multiple graph neural networks, one for each task group.

Negative transfer means that learning multiple tasks with a shared encoder can be worse than single-task learning (STL) for one task, and this has been observed for various data modalities. Often the cause is heterogeneity in the input features or in the dataset sizes. Much less is known about graph data. One study and another study identify structural differences for transfer learning on graphs that come from the graph diffusion process. These structural differences can cause negative interference in multitask learning too. So building multitask graph neural networks needs better modeling of the structural differences between tasks. This modeling could also be used to identify task grouping.

The classical multitask learning literature studied task relatedness through heuristics and from theoretical perspectives. But these results do not naturally apply to nonlinear neural networks. A naive way to optimize multitask learning performance is to search through all the possible combinations of tasks and select the best subset. This is costly to compute when there are many tasks. Prior work computes pairwise task affinity scores by training one model for each pair of tasks, and approximates higher-order task affinities by averaging the first-order affinity scores. Other methods compute first-order task affinities using gradient similarity. These methods are much more efficient than naive search, but they ignore the higher-order relationships among tasks, such as combining more than two tasks. This is critical because higher-order task affinities can be more complex. We observe that they cannot be reliably predicted from the first-order affinity scores (cf. Figure 5, Section 5.1), since transfer relationships are not monotone or submodular, which means adding more task data does not necessarily help performance (see Figure 4, Section 3.2). Also, computing all the pairwise affinities naively requires fitting T^{2} models given T tasks, which is costly even for tens of tasks.

The main contribution of this paper is an efficient algorithm that clusters tasks into similar groups while taking into account higher-order transfer relationships. We can compare the performance of a multitask model, like a GNN trained on all tasks, against several multitask GNNs that are each trained for one task group. Section 5 shows that this approach gives the best results among a wide set of baselines on various real-world datasets. Our method can be seen as a boosting procedure and can be used on top of any graph learning algorithm.

- Main contribution
  - efficient algorithm to cluster tasks into groups with higher-order transfer
  - GNN on all tasks vs several multitask GNNs, one per group
  - Section 5: best results among many baselines; boosting procedure, on top of any graph learning algorithm
- Approach (Figure 1)
  - \theta_{i,j}: how well j transfers to i with other tasks present; like random-forest feature importance
  - spectral clustering on [\theta_{i,j}]_{T\times T}, maximize within-group affinity
  - estimation: O(T^{2}) naive vs O(T) sampling; n=O(T) subsets of size \alpha (\alpha=5)
  - f_{i}(S) holdout loss of task i given S; \theta_{i,j} = average over subsets including i,j
- Theory
  - stochastic block model style setting; planted model -> block-diagonal [\theta_{i,j}]_{T\times T}; spectral clustering recovers structure
- Contributions: affinity score + O(T) sampling; spectral clustering with recovery guarantees; experiments on community detection and molecular graph datasets
- Organization: Sec 2-6, Appendix A proofs, Appendix B extra experiments

This modeling could also be used to identify task grouping.

Other methods compute first-order task affinities using gradient similarity. These methods are much more efficient than naive search, but they ignore the higher-order relationships among tasks, such as combining more than two tasks. This is critical because higher-order task affinities can be more complex. We observe that they cannot be reliably predicted from the first-order affinity scores (cf. Figure 5, Section 5.1), since transfer relationships are not monotone or submodular, which means adding more task data does not necessarily help performance (see Figure 4, Section 3.2). Also, computing all the pairwise affinities naively requires fitting T^{2} models given T tasks, which is costly even for tens of tasks.

The main contribution of this paper is an efficient algorithm that clusters tasks into similar groups while taking into account higher-order transfer relationships. We can compare the performance of a multitask model, like a GNN trained on all tasks, against several multitask GNNs that are each trained for one task group. Section 5 shows that this approach gives the best results among a wide set of baselines on various real-world datasets. Our method can be seen as a boosting procedure and can be used on top of any graph learning algorithm.

Approach. Here we outline the overall procedure (see also Figure 1). Given T tasks, we first compute a task affinity score \theta_{i,j} for each pair of tasks i and j. A higher value of \theta_{i,j} means that task j transfers better to task i, while the presence of other tasks is also accounted for. Conceptually \theta_{i,j} is similar to the feature importance score in random forests when hundreds of other features are available. This higher-order task affinity score can also predict if a set of tasks transfers positively or negatively to a target task. Given the affinity score matrix [\theta_{i,j}]_{T\times T}, we use a spectral clustering algorithm to separate the tasks into similar groups, which are more suitable for joint training. Our algorithm optimizes the sum of task affinity scores within groups through spectral clustering.

Next we describe how to estimate the affinity score matrix. The naive approach computes each entry separately, which needs O(T^{2}) complexity. We design an efficient sampling procedure that only needs O(T) complexity. We sample n=O(T) random subsets from \{1,2,\dots,T\} of a fixed size \alpha (in practice \alpha=5 is enough). We fit an MTL model for each subset and evaluate its prediction loss for each task in the subset. Let f_{i}(S) denote the prediction loss of task i, given a subset S\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,T\}, which we evaluate on a holdout set. So f_{i}(S) measures the information transfer from S to i. Then we compute \theta_{i,j} as the average among all subsets including i,j:

To justify our affinity scores rigorously, we do a theoretical analysis in a setting like a stochastic block model, where the tasks follow a well-separated structure. We prove that under this planted model the affinity score matrix [\theta_{i,j}]_{T\times T} has a block-diagonal structure, with each block corresponding to one cluster. This shows that the spectral clustering algorithm recovers the underlying task structure.

Summary of Contributions. The contribution of this work has three parts. First, we design a task affinity score that measures higher-order task relationships, and we estimate the scores with an efficient sampling procedure that only needs fitting O(T) MTL models. Second, we propose a spectral clustering step that finds task groups based on the affinity score matrix. We give recovery guarantees for this clustering procedure and show that the affinity scores can provably group related tasks in a planted model. Third, we validate the benefit of our boosting approach with various community detection and molecular graph prediction datasets. The experiments show that our approach improves test accuracy over different community detection and MTL baselines.

Organization. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 outlines related work. Section 3 gives empirical grounding for the claim that it is crucial for MTL on graphs to account for negative transfer among tasks. Section 4 describes our boosting procedure, and Section 5 is a thorough empirical study of its performance. Section 6 describes the theoretical analysis of our algorithm. Appendix A has complete proofs for our theoretical results, and Appendix B has additional experimental results left out of the main text.

These results do not naturally apply to nonlinear neural networks. A naive solution for optimizing multitask learning performance is to search through all possible combinations of tasks to select the best subset, which is costly to compute for a large number of tasks. Prior work [17] computes pairwise task affinity scores by training one model for every pair of tasks and approximates higher-order task affinities by averaging first-order affinity scores. [15,18] compute first-order task affinities using gradient similarity. These methods are much more efficient than naive search, but they ignore higher-order relationships among tasks, such as combining more than two tasks. This is critical, as higher-order task affinities can exhibit more complexities. We observe that they cannot be reliably predicted from first-order affinity scores (cf. Figure 5, Section 5.1), since transfer relationships are not monotone or submodular, meaning that adding more task data does not necessarily help performance (see Figure 4, Section 3.2). Moreover, naively computing all pairwise affinities requires fitting T^{2} models given T tasks, which is costly even for tens of tasks.

This paper's main contribution is an efficient algorithm to cluster tasks into similar groups while accounting for higher-order transfer relationships. One can compare the performance of a multitask model, such as a GNN trained on all tasks, against several multitask GNNs, each trained for one task group. Section 5 shows that this approach yields the best results among a wide set of baselines on various real-world datasets. Our method can be viewed as a boosting procedure [19] and can be used on top of any graph learning algorithm.

Approach. We outline the overall procedure; see also Figure 1 for an illustration. Given T tasks, we first compute a task affinity score \theta_{i,j} for every pair of tasks i and j. A higher value of \theta_{i,j} indicates that task j transfers better to task i, while also accounting for the presence of other tasks. Conceptually, \theta_{i,j} is similar to the feature importance score in random forests when hundreds of other features are available. This higher-order task affinity score can also predict whether a set of tasks transfers positively or negatively to a target task. Given the affinity score matrix [\theta_{i,j}]_{T\times T}, we use a spectral clustering algorithm [20,21] to separate tasks into similar groups that are more suitable for joint training. Specifically, our algorithm optimizes the sum of task affinity scores within groups through spectral clustering.

Next, we describe how to estimate the affinity score matrix. A naive approach computes each entry individually, requiring O(T^{2}) complexity. We design an efficient sampling procedure that only requires O(T) complexity. Concretely, we sample n=O(T) random subsets from \{1,2,\dots,T\} of a fixed size \alpha (in practice, \alpha=5 suffices). We fit an MTL model for each subset and evaluate its prediction loss for each task in the subset; let f_{i}(S) denote the prediction loss of task i given a subset S\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,T\}, evaluated on a holdout set. Thus, f_{i}(S) measures the information transfer from S to i. Then, we compute \theta_{i,j} as the average among all subsets including i,j:

To rigorously justify our affinity scores, we conduct a theoretical analysis in a stochastic block model style setting, where tasks follow a well-separated structure. We prove that under this planted model, the affinity score matrix [\theta_{i,j}]_{T\times T} exhibits a block-diagonal structure, with each block corresponding to one cluster. This characterization shows that the spectral clustering algorithm recovers the underlying task structure.

Summary of Contributions. The contribution of this work is threefold. First, we design a task affinity score to measure higher-order task relationships and estimate the scores with an efficient sampling procedure that only requires fitting O(T) MTL models. Second, we propose a spectral clustering step to find task groups based on the affinity score matrix. We provide recovery guarantees for this clustering procedure and show that the affinity scores can provably group related tasks in a planted model. Third, we validate the benefit of our boosting approach on various community detection and molecular graph prediction datasets. The experimental results show that our approach improves test accuracy over different community detection and MTL baselines.

Organization. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. We first outline related work in Section 2. In Section 3, we provide empirical grounding for the claim that accounting for negative transfer among tasks is crucial for MTL on graphs. Our boosting procedure is described in Section 4, followed by a thorough empirical study of its performance in Section 5. In Section 6, we describe the theoretical analysis of our algorithm. Appendix A provides complete proofs for our theoretical results, and Appendix B describes additional experimental results left out of the main text.
